evidence_quotes.quote: The population of interest were service providers in five sectors that were identified and described in a prior data collection exercise on governance diaries data collection, as priorities and unmet needs [31]. The sectors included education, healthcare, water, sanitation, and solid waste management.

Structure owners would initiate locking water points and toilet facilities for use by specific individuals who had fully paid for the services requirement in their structures, without interference by government officials like public health officers. As such, without the external actors, water, health, solid waste management (SWM), and sanitation service providers would set boundaries on services to clients until they could pay as agreed.
We implemented a framework analysis [35], informed by the Ostrom’s theory [36].

“Those offering sanitation services in public toilets and do not have guidelines on how much it cost to use the facility, leads to many challenges including not using a facility when needed or being forced to get into debts for using the facility.

as you move around, you will see long queues in health facilities, water points and sometimes at the sanitation point. On meetings that we conduct here, you hear issues raised related to misuse of resources and a lack of transparency all through”

criterion_notes.c1: Examines informal service provision and resident access across five basic service sectors—explicitly including water and sanitation alongside education, healthcare, and solid waste management—in two urban informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, the study directly analyzes formal and informal governance arrangements in urban informal settlements using Ostrom's institutional design principles. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it examines concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing water and sanitation access: boundary and payment-enforcement rules (structure owners and providers locking water points and toilet facilities to exclude non-paying users), graduated sanctions (denial of service access, forced eviction, or reporting rule violators to chiefs and police), informal vendor entry-approval rules among water vendors, flexible payment accommodations, and the absence or ambiguity of formal tariff/pricing and operational rules (e.g., unguided public toilet fees leading to non-use or household debt, and inflexible bureaucracies/land-tenure barriers).
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative empirical study collecting and analyzing 40 in-depth interviews (36 informal service providers, including 8 water and 8 sanitation providers, and 4 local leaders) conducted March–May 2022 using framework analysis in NVivo 12. Per protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal/institutional empirical studies are included for mechanism synthesis even without quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative empirical outcomes directly relevant to service access, exclusion, availability, and affordability: physical exclusion/denial of access via locked water points and toilets until payment is made or as a sanction for violations, non-use of public toilets when needed or incurring debt due to missing tariff guidelines, long queues at water and sanitation points, and user-provider conflicts over payment at water kiosks.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (40 purposively sampled informal service providers and community leaders operating in Korogocho and Viwandani informal settlements, Nairobi), exposure (informal self-governance rules—boundaries, payment accommodations, monitoring, sanctions, vendor entry rules—and formal policy ambiguity), outcome (qualitative water and sanitation access, exclusion, queues, and affordability/debt), and study design (participatory qualitative interview study) are all clearly identified.

study_design: Participatory qualitative study using in-depth interviews analyzed with thematic framework analysis guided by Ostrom's common-pool resource design principles
population_and_sample: 40 purposively selected participants across two urban informal settlements (Korogocho and Viwandani) in Nairobi, Kenya: 36 long-standing informal service providers (Table 2: 8 water, 8 sanitation, 8 education, 4 healthcare, and 8 solid waste management; text Section 2.3 inconsistently prints n=2 for water per site) and 4 local/community leaders. Unit of analysis: informal service providers and settlement-level service governance arrangements.
exposure: Informal self-governance rules (boundary and payment exclusion rules, payment accommodations, vendor entry approval rules, monitoring, and graduated sanctions) and unclear/ambiguous formal service-delivery and pricing policies
outcome: Qualitative accounts of water and sanitation service access, exclusion/denial of access (locked water points and toilets for non-payment or rule violations), non-use and user debt at public toilets lacking pricing guidelines, conflicts at water kiosks, and queues at water and sanitation points
rationale: This primary qualitative empirical study (40 in-depth interviews in Korogocho and Viwandani informal settlements, Nairobi, Kenya) examines water and sanitation service provision alongside three other basic services. It satisfies both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 by investigating concrete institutional and rule-type mechanisms governing access—including payment-based boundary exclusion (locking water points and toilets), graduated sanctions (denial of service and eviction), informal water-vendor entry rules, payment accommodations, and missing/ambiguous pricing guidelines for public toilets—and links them to access, exclusion, queue/availability, and affordability/debt outcomes. Per protocol rules, qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis despite lacking quantitative effect estimates.
